new_statements.quote: Toda palabra zapoteca de más de una sílaba tiene una sílaba acentuada. Las palabras aumentadas por afijos multisilábicos pueden tener dos o tres sílabas acentuadas. El acento prosódico por lo general cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz. Si ésta no es la penúltima sílaba o si los sufijos cambia la posición de ésta a la que no es la penúltima se escribe el acento. [...] Los prefijos y sufijos de una sílaba del verbo son átonos [...] Los prefijos y sufijos de una sílaba del sustantivo tampoco llevan acento. [...] Los prefijos de dos sílabas llevan su propio acento en la primera sílaba. [...] Los préstamos del español al zapoteco conservan el acento en la misma sílaba que en español.
new_statements.translation: Every Zapotec word of more than one syllable has a stressed syllable. Words extended by polysyllabic affixes may have two or three stressed syllables. Prosodic stress generally falls on the first syllable of the root. If this is not the penultimate syllable, or if suffixes shift it to a position that is not the penult, the accent is written. [...] The monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes of the verb are unstressed [...] The monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes of the noun likewise bear no stress. [...] Disyllabic prefixes carry their own stress on their first syllable. [...] Loans from Spanish into Zapotec keep the stress on the same syllable as in Spanish.
new_statements.citation: Earl, Robert. 2011. Gramática del Zapoteco de Tabaa. Draft grammar sketch (117 pp.), SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 40770, Bartholomew Collection of Unpublished Materials, SIL International Mexico Branch.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is morphologically anchored: it falls on the first syllable of the root; monosyllabic inflectional prefixes and suffixes never take stress. The orthography treats penultimate position as the default outcome (accent mark written only when the root-initial stressed syllable is not the penult), so in typical root+monosyllabic-suffix words stress surfaces on the penult. When an aspect prefix fuses with a vowel-initial root the fused first syllable is stressed (ga-+aza-beß > gázabeß). Stressed vowels lengthen before a simple (lenis/voiced) consonant and stay short before a double (fortis) consonant, a cluster, or a word-final consonant.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary ranking is given, but disyllabic prefixes (xele-, gule-, xulu-, belexe-, dxele-) 'llevan su propio acento en la primera sílaba' (unwritten), and words built with several disyllabic affixes can carry two or three stresses, each on the first syllable of the affix/root (e.g. Dxéle-dá-lýn-técaze-beß-baß).
new_statements.exceptions: 'por lo general' hedge; Spanish loanwords retain Spanish stress position (búrrodauß, máltýdxaß); fusion of aspect prefix with vowel-initial root puts stress on the word's first syllable; vowel sequences: accent may fall on the first or second vowel of a two-vowel sequence (cúa vs. xelúa na, subexíaj).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (morphological word including affixes), illustrated with citation forms and orthographic conventions. The language also has tone, which this sketch treats only in passing: fn. 9 refers to 'tonos altos y bajos' distinguishing verb-root classes, and polar questions are formed with 'un tono alto en el sílabo acentuado' (p. ~57), i.e. tone interacts with the stressed syllable; there is no dedicated tone section in the phonology chapter (§0.1-0.5 cover vowels, consonants, fortis/lenis, syllable types, stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'el zapoteco de Tabáa' (San Juan Tabaá, distrito de Villa Alta, Sierra Norte de Oaxaca) = Glottolog taba1268 / ISO zat exactly; no dialect mismatch. Author notes some inter-speaker variation only in the realisation of the vowel u/o.

sources.note: §0.5 'El acento' (pp. 6-8): every polysyllabic word has a stressed syllable; prosodic stress generally falls on the first syllable of the root; monosyllabic verb/noun prefixes and suffixes are unstressed; disyllabic prefixes carry their own stress on their first syllable (words with polysyllabic affixes can have 2-3 stresses); Spanish loans keep Spanish stress; stressed vowel lengthens before a simple (lenis) consonant; orthographic accent written only when the root stress is not on the penult. Tone only mentioned in passing (fn. 9 'tonos altos y bajos'; yes/no questions marked by 'tono alto…
